# When observations remember each other {#sec-appendix-dependence}

You have met this problem five times; here is its name.
In @sec-principles-experimental-design it was called **pseudoreplication**: fifty academy players assessed at ten sessions each do not make 500 observations, because the repeated assessments of a given player are not independent of each other.
In @sec-one-prop-norm it was the cluster-sample caveat: shots logged from a cluster sample of matches (@sec-samp-methods) are not independent, and the suitable methods were declared "beyond the scope of even most second or third courses in statistics."
In @sec-tech-cond-linmod it was the fourth panel of the residual gallery: sixty consecutive days of one player's GPS training load, residuals snaking above and below the line because the observations remember each other.
In the chapter 24 exercise solutions (@sec-exercise-solutions-24) it was the quiet note that 62 team-match rows come in pairs — two teams per match, and opponents' performances in the same match are not fully independent of one another.
And in @sec-chp26-review it was the book's closing confession: shots nest within matches, matches within teams — structure our independence conditions politely ignored.
The name for all five is **dependence** — in the time-ordered case, *autocorrelation*; in the nested case, *clustering* — and this appendix does the one thing the five warnings never did: it shows you, with real numbers, exactly how much it costs to ignore.

## Sixty days that remember each other {#sec-appendix-dep-ar1}

Rigor first.
The gallery panel in @sec-tech-cond-linmod described a training load that "drifts like a random walk: today's load is yesterday's plus a nudge."
A pure random walk keeps *all* of yesterday — it wanders without a home value, so "the player's long-run mean load" does not even exist as a target.
To study estimation we pull the memory back below one: a series that keeps *most* of yesterday but is always tugged back toward a home value.

::: {.callout-important}
A sequence of measurements $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n$ taken in time order is a **first-order autoregressive process**, written **AR(1)**, if each day's value is built from the day before by

$$
y_t = \mu + \phi \, (y_{t-1} - \mu) + \varepsilon_t
$$

The **autocorrelation** of such a series is the correlation between the measurement on one day and the measurement on the next; for an AR(1) process it equals $\phi.$
When $|\phi| < 1$ the series is **stationary**: it fluctuates around the long-run mean $\mu$ forever, so $\mu$ exists and can be estimated.
When $\phi = 1$ the series is the random walk of @sec-tech-cond-linmod's gallery, and there is no long-run mean to estimate.
:::

Take the equation one piece at a time, because two pieces of notation are new.
The subscript $t$ indexes *time*: $y_t$ is the measurement on day $t,$ and $y_{t-1}$ is the measurement the day before.
You have subscripted observations since @sec-explore-numerical — but $x_i$'s subscript only labeled *which* case, and nothing changed if you shuffled the labels.
Here the order is the point: day 7 follows day 6, and the model says so.
The Greek letter $\phi$ ("phi") is the **memory coefficient**: the fraction of yesterday's deviation from the long-run mean $\mu$ (recall $\mu$ from @sec-explore-numerical) that survives into today.
And $\varepsilon_t$ is the day's fresh nudge — the same population error term $\varepsilon$ you met in @sec-tech-cond-linmod, drawn independently each day with mean 0 and standard deviation $\sigma.$

Now the constructed scenario, seeded and visible as always.
A Northbridge midfielder's daily training load arrives from the sports-science desk as a single figure in arbitrary units (AU).
We build him a 60-day block with a long-run mean of $\mu = 600$ AU, a memory coefficient of $\phi = 0.8$ — strong but stationary, in the neighborhood of the $0.85$ day-to-day correlation the @sec-tech-cond-linmod panel showed — and daily nudges with $\sigma = 60$ AU.
One algebraic fact makes the code below honest: a stationary AR(1) series fluctuates around $\mu$ with long-run standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt{1-\phi^2} = 60/\sqrt{1-0.64} = 60/0.6 = 100$ AU, so we draw day 1 from that long-run distribution rather than letting the first morning be artificially special.

```r
simulate_player <- function(n_days = 60, mu = 600, phi = 0.8, sigma = 60) {
  load <- numeric(n_days)
  load[1] <- mu + rnorm(1, 0, sigma / sqrt(1 - phi^2))
  for (t in 2:n_days) {
    load[t] <- mu + phi * (load[t - 1] - mu) + rnorm(1, 0, sigma)
  }
  load
}

set.seed(9001)
load_60 <- simulate_player()

round(c(mean = mean(load_60), sd = sd(load_60),
        day_to_day_cor = cor(load_60[-1], load_60[-60])), 4)
#>           mean             sd day_to_day_cor
#>       604.1461       107.6054         0.8253
```

The series behaves as designed: it averages $604.1$ AU against a true $\mu$ of 600, its standard deviation of $107.6$ AU sits near the theoretical 100, and the correlation between each day and the next is $0.8253$ — each day carries about four-fifths of the day before.
These are sixty numbers from one body, and they remember each other.

## The naive standard error {#sec-appendix-dep-naive}

Suppose the club's analyst — not yet a reader of this appendix — wants to report the player's 60-day mean load with its uncertainty.
Recall from @sec-one-mean-math that the standard error of a sample mean is $SE = s/\sqrt{n}.$
Sixty observations, standard deviation in hand:

```r
naive_se <- sd(load_60) / sqrt(60)
round(naive_se, 4)
#> [1] 13.8918
```

So the analyst reports $\bar{x} = 604.1$ AU with a standard error of $13.9$ AU, and — following the recipe of @sec-se — an approximate 95% interval of $604.1 \pm 1.96 \times 13.9,$ or roughly $(576.9,\ 631.4)$ AU.
It looks impeccable.
Every symbol is used correctly.
And it is wrong, because $s/\sqrt{n}$ was derived under a condition this data violates in its very construction: that the $n$ observations are independent.

## One thousand parallel players {#sec-appendix-dep-replicates}

The standard error of $\bar{x}$ has a definition that does not care about our formulas: it is the standard deviation of $\bar{x}$ across independent replications of the whole study.
Simulation lets us buy what reality never sells — the replications themselves.
We generate 1,000 *independent* players, each with their own 60-day AR(1) block from the same process, and look at how much their 60-day means actually vary.

```r
set.seed(9002)
mean_60 <- replicate(1000, mean(simulate_player()))

true_sd <- sd(mean_60)
round(c(true_sd = true_sd, naive_se = naive_se,
        ratio = true_sd / naive_se), 4)
#>  true_sd naive_se    ratio
#>  38.0533  13.8918   2.7393
```

The 60-day means of genuinely independent replicate players spread with a standard deviation of $38.1$ AU.
The naive formula said $13.9.$
The truth is $2.74$ times larger than the report.

Turn that ratio into an interval and the damage is plain: the honest 95% interval is $604.1 \pm 1.96 \times 38.1,$ roughly $(529.6,\ 678.7)$ AU — while the analyst shipped $(576.9,\ 631.4).$
An interval built 2.7 times too narrow does not cover the truth 95% of the time; it fails far more often than its label admits, while looking exactly as authoritative on the page.

Why does the formula fail?
Because $s/\sqrt{60}$ prices the data as sixty independent pieces of evidence, and correlated days are not.
Each new day mostly repeats what yesterday already told you, so sixty remembered days carry the information of far fewer independent ones.
The ratio tells us how many.
Since the standard error of a mean shrinks with $\sqrt{n},$ an error inflated by a factor of $2.74$ means the *effective* sample size is smaller by that factor squared:

```r
round(60 / (true_sd / naive_se)^2, 1)
#> [1] 8
```

Sixty correlated days carried the information of roughly **eight independent days**.[^dep-neff]
The analyst's $n = 60$ was a headcount, not an evidence count — the same exaggeration @sec-principles-experimental-design called pseudoreplication when it was 50 players masquerading as 500 assessments.

[^dep-neff]: The seeded estimate; the algebra agrees. For a long AR(1) series the effective sample size tends to $n \times (1-\phi)/(1+\phi) = 60 \times 0.2/1.8 \approx 6.7,$ and the exact finite-length value for these settings is about 7 — either way, nowhere near 60.

::: {.callout-tip title="Check your understanding"}
The naive standard error used $n = 60.$
Would the analyst's report have been *more* honest or *less* honest if the player's memory coefficient had been $\phi = 0.95$ instead of $0.8$?
And in which direction does the error push every p-value computed from such data?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Less honest.
A larger $\phi$ means each day repeats more of the day before, so the same 60 rows carry even less independent information — at $\phi = 0.95$ the long-run effective sample size is about $60 \times 0.05/1.95 \approx 1.5$ days' worth — and the naive $s/\sqrt{60}$ understates the truth by an even larger factor.
The direction of the damage is always the same: standard errors too small, intervals too narrow, and test statistics too large, so p-values come out too eager — the analysis declares differences statistically discernible on evidence that does not exist.
:::

That is the whole indictment, and it is the exact failure this book's independence conditions were guarding against every time they appeared: on remembered data, naive standard errors are too small, intervals are too narrow, and p-values are too eager.
The GPS panel of @sec-tech-cond-linmod was not a stylistic warning about ugly residual plots; it was this appendix's arithmetic, waiting.

## What the remedies are called {#sec-appendix-dep-remedies}

Three families of remedy exist, in ascending order of machinery.

**Aggregate to plausibly independent units.**
Collapse the dependent rows into one number per unit that *can* be treated as independent, and analyze those.
This is the one remedy you already own — and the book itself used the dodge repeatedly without ceremony: shots were aggregated into `team_match` totals before the regressions of @sec-model-slr and @sec-inf-model-slr, and @sec-inference-paired-means folded each team's pressured and unpressured shots into a single within-team difference precisely so that the 22 differences, one per team, could stand as the independent observations.
Aggregation spends data to buy validity: our midfielder's 60 days collapse to one honest mean per block, and you need more players, not more days, to shrink the uncertainty.

**Cluster-robust standard errors.**
Keep the row-level model, but repair the variance estimate by letting observations within the same cluster (player, match, team) be arbitrarily correlated when computing the standard errors.
The coefficients stay; the false precision goes.

**Multilevel (hierarchical, mixed) models.**
Put the structure into the model itself: a level for the player, a level for the match, so that each source of variation is estimated rather than ignored — this is the "player as a level" phrasing you will meet immediately in the literature, and the machinery behind @sec-chp26-review's parting sentence about shots nesting within matches and matches within teams.
The reading path for all three families — Gelman and Hill first — is laid out in @sec-appendix-further.

One closing paragraph, analyst to analyst.
A club's data almost always remembers itself: the same player wears the vest every morning, the same eleven take the shots, the two teams in every match share its weather, its referee, and its scoreline.
You are not yet equipped to fit multilevel models — this book never pretended otherwise — but you are fully equipped, today, for the honest move: aggregate to units you can defend as independent, state that choice in the frame sentence right next to your pens-in-or-out declaration, and price the cost in sample size openly.
An interval on eight honest observations is worth more to Marta Vidal than an interval on sixty remembered ones, because the first one means what it says.
